test.title: How a city learned to cycle

paragraphs.text: In 1990 fewer than one in fifty journeys in the city of Veldhaven were made by bicycle. Today the figure is almost one in four, a change that has attracted visitors from transport departments around the world.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The change did not begin with cyclists but with a road accident. In 1994 a lorry killed two children cycling to school, and the protests that followed persuaded the council to build the first separated cycle lanes on the main routes into the centre.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Separated lanes proved far more effective than painted lines on the road. Surveys showed that many residents, particularly women and older people, had wanted to cycle but felt unsafe sharing space with cars. Once physical barriers were installed, the number of cyclists on those routes doubled within three years.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Not every measure was popular. When the council removed parking spaces to make room for lanes, shop owners protested that they would lose customers. A later study of spending found, however, that cyclists visited local shops more often than drivers, even though they spent less on each visit.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Veldhaven’s planners warn other cities against simply copying their network. The city is flat and compact, and its winters are mild. In hillier or colder places, they suggest, electric bicycles and heated shelters at stations may be needed before large numbers of people switch.
paragraphs.label: E
